name: Singapore Math
line: Singapore Math teaches by half-year book. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review happen at every problem.
description: AMP vs Singapore Math: printed books an adult places and checks. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review are continuous, at every problem.
verdict: Singapore Math is printed books, a half-year book at a time: the adult reads a placement test to choose the book, and the lessons move from objects to pictures to symbols [1][3]. In AMP, assessment and teaching are continuous. Every answer updates the learner's level and sets the next problem, and each problem carries its own hint, lesson and worked answer.

reasons.title: Continuous assessment
reasons.body: AMP has no separate test. It places a learner from their first answers, and every answer after updates the learner's level in that part of math and sets the next problem. Singapore Math places a learner with a placement test for each half-year book. The tests are untimed and not scored. The adult watches how the learner works and which mistakes come up, then picks the book: pass 2A, take 2B [3].

reasons.title: Feedback on every answer
reasons.body: After every answer AMP shows whether it was right, the correct answer and the worked steps. Singapore Math is a set of printed textbooks and workbooks [1]. A learner works on paper, and the adult checks the work [2][3]. Across 40 studies of computer-based feedback, in many ages and subjects, feedback that explains averaged an effect of 0.49, against 0.05 for marking right or wrong only [8].

reasons.title: The problem is the unit
reasons.body: In AMP, everything hangs off the problem: a hint that gives the first step, a lesson with a worked example, a video lesson, the worked answer afterward, and links to the skills it builds on and leads to. In Singapore Math the unit is the half-year book and the lessons in it, which move from concrete objects to pictures to symbols [1][3]. Dimensions Math also has video lessons [1].

reasons.title: Moving on, and going back
reasons.body: In AMP a skill counts when the learner gets it right without help, more than once. Repeated misses send practice back to what the skill builds on. In Singapore Math the adult judges a level from the learner's work, not a score. The placement tests do not cover every topic in a level, and the company tells parents to check the scope and sequence for the rest [3].

reasons.title: Continuous review
reasons.body: In AMP, learned skills come back in ordinary practice, at growing intervals, mixed with other math. Singapore Math calls its approach a "mastery spiral" [1]. We found no review schedule in its published materials [1][3]. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders, mixed practice, which was also spaced, scored 62% a month later on the researchers' own test, against 38% for practice in blocks [9].

reasons.title: A level for each part of math
reasons.body: AMP keeps a separate level for each part of math, from counting through precalculus in one program. A learner further along in geometry than in fractions gets work at both levels. Singapore Math places a learner in one half-year book [3]. Dimensions Math runs from pre-kindergarten through grade 8 [1].

rows.range: Dimensions Math: pre-kindergarten to grade 8. Primary Mathematics in several editions, with placement tests up to grade 6 [1][3].
rows.start: A placement test for each half-year book, untimed and not scored. The adult reads the work and picks the book [3].
rows.teaching: Printed lessons that move from concrete objects to pictures to symbols [1]. Dimensions Math also has video lessons [1].
rows.next: The books' order, a half-year book at a time: pass 2A, take 2B [3].
rows.mastery: Judged by the adult from the learner's work, not a score. Placement tests do not cover every topic in a level [3].
rows.review: A "mastery spiral" [1]. No review schedule found in its published materials [1][3].
rows.print: Printed textbooks and workbooks, not made for one learner [1][2].
rows.adult: Gives the placement test, reads the work to choose the level, and checks the learner's work [2][3].
rows.reports: None found in the pages we read [1].
rows.evidence: No studies met Evidence for ESSA or What Works Clearinghouse standards [6][7]. HMH's Math in Focus, a separate program, is rated Strong [4].

theirs: Singapore Math Inc. brings the Singapore approach to math to U.S. families and schools [1]. Its main series are Dimensions Math, for pre-kindergarten to grade 8, and Primary Mathematics, in several editions [1]. Math in Focus is a different program: a school edition of the Singapore approach, published by Houghton Mifflin Harcourt [5].

The books teach with concrete objects first, then pictures, then symbols, in what the company calls a "mastery spiral" [1]. Each grade comes in two books: A for the first half of the year, B for the second [3]. A family starts with a placement test, untimed and not scored; the adult watches how the learner works, then picks the book [2][3]. Supplements add practice, fluency work and word problems [1].
credit: Concrete objects, then pictures, then symbols [1]. The What Works Clearinghouse guide for elementary math intervention rates concrete and semi-concrete representations as strong evidence [10].
Placement read from the learner's work: how they solve, and which mistakes come up [3].

theirs: As of November 2026, we found no outcome study of Dimensions Math or Primary Mathematics on Singapore Math Inc.'s site, in Evidence for ESSA or in What Works Clearinghouse intervention reports. The home page cites no studies [1]. Evidence for ESSA lists Singapore Math without a rating, because no studies met its inclusion requirements [6]. The What Works Clearinghouse found no studies of Singapore Mathematics, reviewed as Primary Mathematics, that met its standards, in a report dated December 2015 [7].

Evidence for ESSA rates HMH's Math in Focus Strong: four studies, 3,444 students in grades 2 to 5, an average effect size of +0.15 on standardized measures [4]. One study, by Jaciw and colleagues at Empirical Education, is titled as a randomized trial. The others are by the Educational Research Institute of America, listed as HMH reports, and JEM & R LLC [4]. Teachers in the studies had summer training and four whole days of training during the year [4]. The rating is for Math in Focus in schools, not for Singapore Math Inc.'s books [4][6].
ours: Two findings bear on this comparison. Across 40 studies of computer-based feedback, in many ages and subjects, feedback that explains averaged an effect of 0.49, against 0.05 for marking right or wrong only [8]. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders that meets What Works Clearinghouse standards without reservations, mixed practice, which was also spaced, scored 62% a month later on the researchers' own test, against 38% for practice in blocks [9]. AMP applies both at every problem.

AMP's own outcome studies are planned: growth on a national test against hours of use, then comparison groups, then randomized trials. Each will be registered before it starts and published whatever it finds. The research behind each part of AMP is in our report, and AMP is open source.

them: You want to teach math yourself from a book, from objects to pictures to symbols.
amp: You want every answer checked and explained as it is given.
You want assessment, teaching and review in the same practice, with no separate tests.
You want learned skills to keep coming back in practice.
Your learner is at different levels in different parts of math, or ready for algebra.
You want paper workbooks made from your learner's own record.

questions.question: How is AMP different from Singapore Math?
questions.answer: In Singapore Math the adult reads a placement test, picks a half-year book, and checks the work on paper [2][3]. AMP has no separate test: every answer sets the next problem, each problem carries its own teaching, and learned skills return in ordinary practice.

questions.question: Does Singapore Math work?
questions.answer: We found no outcome study of Dimensions Math or Primary Mathematics on Singapore Math Inc.'s site, in Evidence for ESSA or in What Works Clearinghouse intervention reports [1][6][7]. Evidence for ESSA rates HMH's Math in Focus, a separate Singapore-style school program, Strong [4].

questions.question: Can a learner use both?
questions.answer: Yes. They are separate programs. A learner can work from the books and practice in AMP, which places them from their first answers.
